nameStory: The Eyed Brown gets its name from the distinctive eyespots on its wings that look like tiny dark eyes staring back at you. These circular markings, called ocelli by scientists, help startle predators and may redirect attacks away from vital body parts. The 'brown' part is pretty straightforward – these butterflies sport lovely chocolate and tan tones that blend perfectly with their marshy homes.
description: The Eyed Brown is a medium-sized butterfly with soft brown wings decorated with dark eyespots ringed in pale yellow or orange. Its wingspan ranges from about 1.5 to 2 inches across, making it smaller than a Monarch but larger than most skippers. The overall color is a warm chocolate brown with lighter tan patches, giving it an understated elegance. This gentle butterfly has a bouncing, somewhat weak flight pattern that rarely takes it far from its wetland home.

idTips.label: Eyespots
idTips.description: Look for 4-6 dark circular spots with pale rings on the underwings, resembling tiny eyes peering at you. These are most visible when the butterfly is at rest with wings closed.

idTips.label: Brown coloration
idTips.description: Wings are rich chocolate brown above with lighter tan or buff-colored patches that feel velvety to the touch if you examine a specimen closely.

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a distinctive bouncing, somewhat floppy motion, staying low to the ground and rarely venturing far from sedge patches.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized with wings spanning 1.5-2 inches, about the size of a half-dollar coin when fully spread.

idTips.label: Wing texture
idTips.description: Wings have a soft, matte finish rather than the glossy sheen of some other butterflies, with edges that may appear slightly worn even on fresh individuals.

habitat: Eyed Browns are wetland specialists, found in marshes, wet meadows, and the soggy edges of ponds and streams where sedges grow thick. They prefer areas with standing water or consistently moist soil, often in partially shaded spots where cattails and various sedge species create a lush, green carpet. You'll have the best luck finding them in coastal marshes, beaver ponds, and the muddy margins of slow-moving rivers throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active in spring. Look for overwintering caterpillars on sedge plants in marsh areas, though they're quite difficult to spot.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season from late June through August. Adults are most active on warm, humid days, often seen nectaring on marsh flowers or resting on sedge blades with wings closed.
seasonality.fall: Flight season winds down by early September. Mated females lay eggs on sedge plants before the first frost ends the adult season.
seasonality.winter: Only eggs and young caterpillars survive the winter, hidden deep in sedge tussocks where they're completely dormant until spring warmth returns.

funFact: Eyed Brown caterpillars are such picky eaters that they can only survive on specific types of sedges – if you moved one just a few feet away from its host plant to a different sedge species, it would literally starve rather than eat the 'wrong' plant, even though both might look identical to us!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its cousin the Northern Pearly-eye, but Eyed Browns are smaller and lack the pearly-white patch that gives the Pearly-eye its name. Remember: 'Eyed' for eyespots only, 'Pearly-eye' for eyespots plus that distinctive white shimmer.
contextualKnowledge: This butterfly was recently moved from the genus Satyrodes to Lethe, so you might see it listed under either name in older field guides. Both names refer to the same species, but Lethe is the currently accepted scientific name.
compareHints: Compared to the Northern Pearly-eye in the same genus, the Eyed Brown is noticeably smaller and darker, lacking the pearly-white patches that make its relative so distinctive. The Appalachian Brown is more similar in size but typically shows more orange around its eyespots and prefers woodland edges rather than true wetlands. Eyed Browns stick closest to water and have the most subdued, chocolate-brown coloration of the three.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Lethe genus relatives in New England, the Northern Pearly-eye stands out with its silvery-white eyespot rings—the Eyed Brown has yellowish rings around its spots, while the Appalachian Brown has more subdued, less contrasting eyespots.

Compared to its close relatives, the Appalachian Brown has more subdued eyespots than the Northern Pearly-eye (which has large, pearly-white centered spots) and prefers deeper forest shade than the Eyed Brown (which favors wet meadows and marsh edges).
